front: What is the fundamental value F_t in Definition 1.2?
back: The present value at date t of the dividends paid after t: F_t = sum over k of d_(t+k) / (1 + r)^k, for k from 1 to infinity, whenever the series converges. It is a benchmark computed from dividends and the discount rate, not a forecast of any price.

front: Theorem 1.3 (closed form). Hypotheses: A0, r > g and 1 + g > 0; A1, d_s = d_1 (1 + g)^(s-1) for every s >= 1, with d_1 real. What is F_t for every integer t >= 0?
back: F_t = d_1 (1 + g)^t / (r - g) = d_(t+1) / (r - g). In particular F_0 = d_1 / (r - g). The series in Definition 1.2 converges.

front: Theorem 1.3 with hypotheses A0 (r > g, 1 + g > 0) and A1 (d_s = d_1 (1 + g)^(s-1)). What identity do the partial sums S_N(t) satisfy, for every N >= 1?
back: S_N(t) = F_t (1 - q^N) exactly, with q = (1 + g) / (1 + r). Lab 1 Part A checks this in exact arithmetic for N = 10, 60 and 200.
basis: Proof in Section 1 (Theorem 1.3); Lab 1 Part A (exact check)

front: Under A0 (r > g and 1 + g > 0), what range does q = (1 + g) / (1 + r) lie in, and what follows for the partial sums?
back: 0 < q < 1. So q^N tends to 0, and the partial sums converge to F_t.

front: Proposition 1.4 (no finite benchmark). Hypotheses: d_1 > 0, 1 + g > 0, r > -1 and g >= r, with d_s = d_1 (1 + g)^(s-1). What happens to the partial sums S_N(0) as N grows?
back: S_N(0) tends to +infinity. The series in Definition 1.2 does not converge, so Theorem 1.3 does not apply.

front: Definition 2.1: what is the speculative bubble at date t, relative to the benchmark F_t?
back: The gap B_t = P_t - F_t, counted as a bubble only when B_t > 0. The gap is measured in cents. A price with B_t <= 0 has no bubble on this definition.

front: Proposition 2.2. Hypotheses: d_1 > 0; Assumption 1.1 holds with growth rates g < g' and one discount rate r, where r > g, r > g', 1 + g > 0 and 1 + g' > 0. What is the ordering of F_0(g) and F_0(g')?
back: F_0(g) < F_0(g'). So every price P_0 with F_0(g) < P_0 <= F_0(g') has a positive gap under g and a non-positive gap under g'.

front: Definition 3.1: how is a financial panic defined?
back: A sudden, collective demand by holders of financial claims to convert them into money or into assets regarded as safe, in which many claims fall in price together or trading in them stops. The definition names the mechanism only. It states no frequency, trigger or size.
basis: Definition 3.1 (a definition; it states no empirical claim)

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED): under the stated 3 percent growth, in how many of the 13 periods t = 0 to 12 is the price above the fundamental?
back: 9 of 13. This is one seeded draw of the wedges, not an estimate for any market.

front: Lab 1 Part C (SIMULATED): with the same prices and 1 percent growth, in how many of the 13 periods is the price above the alternative fundamental?
back: 13 of 13. The count changes with the assumed growth rate, from 9 of 13 under 3 percent.

front: Is a price above the present value of the dividends a bubble?
back: Only relative to the stated benchmark. With d_1 = 400 cents and r = 9 percent, a price of 6000 cents is above the benchmark under 1 percent growth and below it under 3 percent growth (Proposition 2.2).

front: Does d_1 / (r - g) give the present value of any dividend stream?
back: No. The formula needs (A1), which fixes every dividend from d_1 and g. A stream with d_1 = 400 cents, r = 9 percent and no later dividends has present value 40000/109 cents, which is 367 cents to the nearest cent. The formula gives 6667 cents at g = 3 percent.
basis: Calculation in the canon-breaks list of L01 Section 5; Theorem 1.3 proof uses (A1)

front: With d_1 > 0 and growth at or above the discount rate (g >= r), is the benchmark a finite value?
back: No. Each discounted dividend is at least d_1 / (1 + r), so the partial sums grow without bound and the closed form does not give a finite value (Proposition 1.4).

front: Definition 1.1: what does a gold standard fix, and what does convertibility at the parity require?
back: It fixes a parity kappa > 0, the quantity of gold in grams for one unit of the currency. Convertibility at that parity means the issuer stands ready to buy and sell gold at the parity on demand.

front: Proposition 1.2. Hypothesis (A1): the issuer keeps the parity kappa at every date t. What does one gram of gold cost at date t?
back: 1/kappa units of the currency, at every date t.

front: Does fixing the gold price of the currency fix the price level?
back: No. Proposition 1.2 gives one price, the currency price of gold. Its hypothesis (A1) does not involve the price index P_t, so its conclusion holds whatever path P_t follows.

front: What is the real value V_t of a fixed nominal debt D, in base-date cents?
back: V_t = D P_0 / P_t, where D is the nominal amount in integer cents and P_0 is the base value of the price index.

front: Proposition 2.1, part (a). Hypotheses: (A2) D is a fixed positive integer number of cents, paid in full and not renegotiated; (A3) P_t is a positive real number for every date t. What is V_t / V_(t-1) for t >= 1?
back: P_(t-1) / P_t. The factor D P_0 cancels in the ratio.

front: Proposition 2.1, part (b). Hypotheses: (A2) D is a fixed positive integer number of cents, paid in full; (A3) P_t is positive for every date t. What is V_T / V_0 for every T >= 1?
back: P_0 / P_T. The one-period ratios of part (a) telescope.

front: Definition 3.1: what is debt deflation?
back: The rise in the real value V_t of a fixed nominal debt that a fall in the price index P_t produces, with D held fixed.

front: Corollary 3.2. Hypotheses: (A2) and (A3) of Proposition 2.1. For t >= 1, when does the real value rise, V_t > V_(t-1)?
back: If and only if P_t < P_(t-1). A fall in the price index raises the real value of a fixed nominal debt.

front: When the price index falls from P_(t-1) to P_t, by what factor does the real value of the fixed nominal debt change?
back: It is multiplied by P_(t-1) / P_t, which is larger than one. Corollary 3.2 gives the direction of the change, not its size.

front: When prices fall, does a fixed nominal debt become cheaper to repay?
back: No. A fall in P_t raises the real value V_t (Corollary 3.2). In Lab 1 Part C, six periods have a falling index and six have a rising real value, and the two sets of periods are equal.
basis: Corollary 3.2 (T) for the direction; Lab 1 Part C (SIMULATED) for the counts

front: Is the real value of a fixed nominal debt constant over time?
back: No. V_t = D P_0 / P_t changes whenever P_t changes. In Lab 1 Part B the real value differs from its predecessor in each of the 12 periods.
basis: Definition of V_t in Section 2 (T); Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED) for the 12 periods

front: Lab 1 (SIMULATED): does the identity V_t / V_(t-1) = P_(t-1) / P_t hold on the simulated path, and do the falling-index and rising-real-value periods coincide?
back: The identity holds exactly at all 12 dates. Six periods each have a falling index and a rising real value, and the two sets of periods are equal.
basis: Lab 1 Parts B and C (SIMULATED, one seeded path)

front: Assumption 1.1 (parity and deflation). What is the model's price index P_t, and what happens after period m?
back: P_t = (1 - delta)^min(t, m), with P_0 = 1, for 0 <= m <= H and 0 < delta < 1. The index falls by the fraction delta in each period on parity and is flat after period m.

front: Definition 2.1: what is leverage L_t in the model?
back: The ratio L_t = V_t / N_t of the real debt V_t to the borrower's net worth N_t.

front: In the model, what is the external-finance premium psi_t?
back: The rise in the extra cost of outside funds above its baseline: psi_t = phi (L_t - L_0), with slope phi > 0 (Assumption 1.3).

front: State the credit channel of a depression, as the model's chain (Definition 2.2).
back: A fall in the price index raises the real value of the fixed nominal debt (A1 and A2). The rise lowers borrower net worth one for one (A2). Higher leverage raises the premium (A3). The premium lowers output by f_t, a fraction of baseline output (A3). The chain describes the model and no economy outside it.

front: Lemma 3.1. Hypotheses: C = N_0 + D; for D <= x < C, ell(x) = x / (C - x); Assumptions 1.2 and 1.3. What does L_t equal, and is ell increasing?
back: L_t = ell(V_t) whenever V_t < C, and L_0 = D / N_0. The function ell is strictly increasing on [D, C).

front: Proposition 3.2(a). Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3, including the inequality V_m < N_0 + D of Assumption 1.2, with V_m = D (1 - delta)^(-m). What bound holds for the real debt over the horizon?
back: V_t <= V_m for every t from 0 to H. For t at most m, V_t = D (1 - delta)^(-t), which is strictly increasing when m >= 1. For t at least m, V_t = V_m.

front: Proposition 3.2(b). Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3. What is depth(m) in closed form?
back: depth(m) = beta phi (ell(V_m) - ell(D)) = beta phi (V_m / (N_0 + D - V_m) - D / N_0), with V_m = D (1 - delta)^(-m).

front: Proposition 3.2(c). Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3. In which period is the maximum of the output fall first attained?
back: At t = m. When m >= 1, no earlier period attains the maximum.

front: Under Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3, what is depth(0)?
back: Zero. With m = 0, P_t = 1 for every t, so V_t = D, L_t = L_0 and the premium is zero in every period.

front: Corollary 3.3. Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3 for two parity durations m' and m with 0 <= m' < m <= H. What is the ordering of depth(m') and depth(m)?
back: depth(m') < depth(m): a longer parity duration gives a strictly deeper fall. In Lab 1, economy X (m = 12) is therefore deeper than economy Y (m' = 4) under these assumptions.

front: Corollary 3.4. Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3 for two parity durations m' and m with 1 <= m' < m <= H. What is depth(m) / depth(m')?
back: (ell(V_m) - ell(D)) / (ell(V_m') - ell(D)). The right-hand side does not depend on beta or phi.

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, phi = beta = 1): what is economy X's output depth, and when is it first reached?
back: 9.20 percent of baseline output, first reached at t = 12.
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED model values, printed to two decimals)

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, phi = beta = 1): what is economy Y's output depth, and when is it first reached?
back: 2.69 percent of baseline output, first reached at t = 4.
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED model values, printed to two decimals)

front: Lab 1 Part D (SIMULATED): what is the ratio of the depths of X to Y for beta phi = 1, and does it change across the products 1/2, 1 and 3?
back: 3.4260 for beta phi = 1. The same 3.4260 is printed for each of the products 1/2, 1 and 3, as Corollary 3.4 requires.

front: Definition 4.1: what is a lender of last resort?
back: A central bank that lends against collateral to institutions that are solvent but illiquid. Solvent means the assets, valued as the lender values them, cover the liabilities. Illiquid means the institution cannot meet its payments from its own resources in the time available.

front: Definition 4.1: what is a central bank?
back: The public institution that issues the monetary base.

front: Does Proposition 3.2 say what a lender of last resort does to the premium?
back: No. Assumption 1.2 has no lending term, and Assumption 1.3 has no term through which a facility changes the premium of a solvent borrower. The proposition therefore says nothing about a facility.

front: Does the model show that bank failures caused the depth?
back: No. The model has no bank, no failure and no default, which Assumption 1.2 excludes. The proof of Proposition 3.2 uses none of these events.
basis: Assumption 1.2 and the proof of Proposition 3.2

front: Does economy X's larger depth show that holding parity makes output fall further?
back: No. The ordering follows from the parity durations of 12 and 4 that Assumption 1.1 sets. The model cannot say whether holding parity causes a deeper fall.
basis: Proof of Corollary 3.3; Lab 1 Part B

front: Does a lender of last resort lend to any firm that asks?
back: No. Definition 4.1 requires collateral and limits lending to institutions that are solvent but illiquid.

front: Is the 9.20 percent depth in Lab 1 a measured fall in output?
back: No. It is a SIMULATED model value under Assumption 1.3 with beta = 1, and no output series enters the lab. Changing beta changes the depth in proportion, through the factor beta phi (Proposition 3.2(b)).

front: What does the honest-pending note say about the data for the lab in L03?
back: The curriculum names embedded data for this lab, but no redistributable historical series for gold-standard adherence or output depth is embedded. The lab therefore runs a stylised model, labelled SIMULATED, and its numbers are the model's.

front: Definition 1.1: what is the monthly log change at month t?
back: ell_t = ln(x_t / x_(t-1)), the natural logarithm of the ratio of two consecutive rates. It is a change per month and is not annualized.

front: Definition 1.1: what is the dispersion of a window of monthly log changes, and when is it defined?
back: The sample standard deviation of the n changes, with denominator n - 1, about their mean. It is defined only when n >= 2.

front: Proposition 1.2 (telescoping). Assuming (A1): the rates x_t are positive for every month from a to b, with a < b. What is the sum of ell_t for t from a + 1 to b?
back: ln(x_b / x_a). The sum has b - a terms.

front: Is Lab 1's check of Proposition 1.2 an exact check in floating-point arithmetic?
back: No. Proposition 1.2 is an exact identity in real numbers. The lab checks it in floating point to a tolerance of 10^-12, which confirms the computation to that tolerance only.
basis: Remark 1.3; the tolerance SUM_TOLERANCE = 1e-12 in the Lab 1 code

front: Proposition 2.2 (zero dispersion in the model). Hypotheses: (A2), x_t = kappa at every month of the window, with kappa > 0, and at least two monthly changes. What are the monthly log changes and the dispersion of the window?
back: Every monthly log change is 0, and the dispersion is 0.

front: In this lesson, what is a Bretton Woods system?
back: A model class: an anchor currency, one foreign currency, a parity kappa > 0 and a market rate x_t, together with (A2), the parity held at every month. It states no historical parity, participant or end.

front: Lab 1 Part B (embedded GBP column): which months in window one have an exactly zero monthly change, and how many of its changes are nonzero?
back: Three months: 1976-07, 2012-07 and 2019-11. So 665 of the 668 changes are nonzero.
basis: Lab 1 Part B (embedded fx_monthly GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the dispersion of window one, 1971-02 to 2026-09, and how many monthly changes does it hold?
back: 0.027935 per month, from 668 monthly log changes (sample standard deviation with denominator 667).
basis: Lab 1 Part C (embedded fx_monthly GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the dispersion of window two, 2000-01 to 2026-09, and how many monthly changes does it hold?
back: 0.024700 per month, from 321 monthly log changes.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (embedded fx_monthly GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part D: what is window two's dispersion as a multiple of window one's, and what is window two minus window one?
back: 0.8842 times window one. The difference is -0.003236.
basis: Lab 1 Part D (embedded fx_monthly GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the largest absolute monthly log change in window two, in which month, and with what sign?
back: 0.096575 in absolute value, at 2008-10. The signed value is -0.096575.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (embedded fx_monthly GBP column)

front: Does a currency with a parity have no monthly change in its recorded rate?
back: Not in a recorded series. Proposition 2.2 gives zero change for the model under (A2). In Lab 1 Part B, the recorded GBP column has 665 nonzero changes among the 668 in window one.

front: Does a smaller dispersion in window two show that the currency became calmer because of a regime change?
back: No. Lab 1 computes two sample standard deviations and their difference. It computes no test and names no cause, and the window start is a convention.
basis: Lab 1 Part D; Problem E3 (the code contains no test)

front: Is the monthly log change the same number as the simple percent change?
back: No. A rise from 1.00 to 1.10 has a simple change of 0.10 and a log change of ln 1.1 = 0.095310 to six decimals, a difference of 0.004690.

front: Does calling the model a Bretton Woods system state what the historical arrangement was?
back: No. Definition 2.1 defines a model class. The lesson states no historical fact about the arrangement's parities, participants or end, and Section 4 lists the open items.

front: Why does window two start at 2000-01 in Lab 1?
back: It is the first month from which the other two embedded snapshots, fx_daily and ust_daily, have data, since both begin on 2000-01-03 in their MANIFEST entries. The start is a convention, and the lab does not test whether the difference survives another start.

front: Which embedded dataset does Lab 1 read, and what are its coverage and limits?
back: fx_monthly.csv: the Federal Reserve G.5/H.10 noon buying rates in New York, column GBP in US dollars per pound. It has 669 months from 1971-01 to 2026-09, retrieved 2026-10-19. It holds spot rates only, with no interest or forward rates.
